articles.title: Gremlins Sequel Video Brings Back the Best Villain of the Franchise After 42 Years
articles.summary: Two years before Gremlins 3 arrives in theaters, Gizmo and Stripe have been reunited for a new Christmas commercial from AT&T. While Gizmo has made several appearances outside of the movies over the years, it's considerably rarer to see Stripe brought to life in live-action. The villain of the original Gremlins hasn't appeared in a […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Two years before Gremlins 3 arrives in theaters , Gizmo and Stripe have been reunited for a new Christmas commercial from AT&T. While Gizmo has made several appearances outside of the movies over the years, it's considerably rarer to see Stripe brought to life in live-action. The villain of the original Gremlins hasn't appeared in a theatrical movie since 1984. The new commercial even brings back Stripe in his Mogwai form, complete with his signature white mohawk.

The commercial finds the two Mogwai getting along considerably better than they did in Joe Dante's original movie. The pair are hanging out on a couch playing with Samsung devices with a plate of Christmas cookies in front of them. Fortunately, someone in the house is familiar with the rules of owning a Mogwai and takes the cookies away as the clock strikes midnight. Both characters were brought to life using puppets. It's a particularly welcome sight for fans wondering what the creatures will look like when original Gremlins screenwriter Chris Columbus takes over directing duties for the third movie .

Gremlins Has a Long History of Great Television Commercials Selling products with Mogwai is almost as old as the franchise itself. Kids in the 1980s could start their mornings with a bowl of Gremlins cereal. It's pretty funny in retrospect that a movie featuring a creature exploding in a microwave spawned a breakfast cereal marketed to children. Ralston's commercial for the cereal even incorporated the rules from the movie into its sales pitch. The movie's somewhat complicated relationship with its own merchandising would become one of the many things Dante poked fun at in Gremlins 2: The New Batch .

In 2021, Mountain Dew gave fans something they'd been waiting decades to see when the company reunited Zach Galligan with Gizmo for a commercial promoting Mountain Dew Zero Sugar. The commercial found an older Billy Peltzer still living with Gizmo. Despite having spent decades taking care of the little guy, Billy still hasn't learned his lesson when it comes to letting Gizmo near liquids.

What's fun about the Mountain Dew commercial is that it actually builds on the mythology of the movies. The commercial introduces audiences to Billy's daughter, who has a Mogwai of her own. It even includes an aged-up Gizmo, complete with a white-haired goatee. While commercials featuring characters from beloved movies often recreate scenes from those movies, Mountain Dew essentially produced a 30-second legacy sequel to Gremlins .

Between the Mountain Dew and AT&T commercials, fans have gotten a couple of opportunities to see how well the characters work in live-action more than three decades after the release of Gremlins 2 . Fortunately, neither company felt the need to modernize Gizmo's design or abandon the puppetry that made audiences fall in love with the character in the first place. With Columbus planning to utilize practical creature effects in Gremlins 3 , these commercials might be the best indication yet of what fans can expect to see on the big screen on October 6th, 2028.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The relationship between toys and comics is, and has always been, a mutually beneficial one. Think of legendary comic writer Larry Hama’s stint on G.I. Joe in the 1980s or Ralph Macchio’s issues for The Transformers . Pairing up toys and comics gives the opportunity to create a broader fictional universe around a pre-existing concept. This either amplifies the love kids already have for a toy, or it gives a toy that isn’t working another chance. It allows the comic to exist beyond pages, giving kids the opportunity to use their own imaginations on what may happen in the fictional worlds created by these writers.

Toys and comics were further intermingled in the 1980s — a great decade for both toys and comics — when several franchises included mini-comics with the release of individual toy figures. Now seen as valuable collectibles, these mini-comics were just bonuses with the toy when they first arrived. Some lines were more successful than others, launching line after line of mini-comics while others stopped after only three issues. See if you can remember any of these beloved toy-comic mashups below!

Although toy giant Mattel acquired it in 1996, Tyco carved out its own niche in the toy market for a time. Tyco was founded in the 1950s as a producer of toy train kits before moving on to pre-built trains, slot cars, and remote control vehicles. In December of 1987, Tyco launched a toy line known as Dino-Riders. With each dinosaur figure released, kids got a mini-comic. Since it was a new toy, Tyco figured a comic would help market the action figures . According to the comic, Dino-Riders was about the battle between the superhuman Valorians and the humanoid Rulons, set during dinosaur times on Earth.

The comic was sixteen pages long, and Tyco would release two issues of it. The second issue continued the narrative from the first one and was included in each box of the toy’s second, third, and Ice-Age series. The mini-issues were written by regular Tyco freelancer Paul Kirchner. In addition to Dino-Riders , Kirchner wrote for Tyco’s Crash Dummies and Spy-Tech toy lines. It would hardly be his only contribution to toy comics, given his work with G.I. Joe, He-Man, Thundercats, and Power Rangers in the 1980s and 1990s.

Before the company filed for bankruptcy and had its products bought out by Hasbro in 1989, Coleco Industries, known for Cabbage Patch Dolls, created a line of action figures. These figures were known as the Sectaurs , the warriors of Symbion. The warriors of Symbion were humanoids who had insect- and arachnid-like features.

The Sectaurs toys included nine mini-comics with the series released in 1984. From 1985 to 1986, a series of regular comics from Marvel about the Sectaurs was written by Bill Mantlo. Mantlo is perhaps better known for his work on the Micronauts and Rom , along with co-creating Rocket Raccoon and the pair Cloak and Dagger. While each toy’s mini-comic was meant to spotlight the character or playset it came with, some comics were more common than others, such as “The World of Symbion”.

MASK had three mini-comics that came out with the Kenner toys. The comics were randomly included in 1985’s series one boxes, and they were the first comics that were produced for MASK. These comics delved into the world set up by the animated series but brought the characterization, history, and worldbuilding beyond it. The first comic gave MASK a beginning, something that was never given attention in the animated series, while the two other issues told comic-exclusive adventures.

“Flaming Beginnings” had a double storyline, showing the beginning of Matt Tracker’s battle with Mayhem and how he lost his brother Andy, along with present-day Miles Mayhem’s attempt to use a human robot to sabotage Matt Tracker and Bruce Sato. “Monster from VENOM” featured another attack on Matt Trakker and Bruce Sato, this time featuring a Loch Ness Monster-esque creature, while “Assault on Boulder Hill” concluded the saga with yet another of Miles Mayhem’s plans going awry.

Masters of the Universe was a force to be reckoned with during the 1980s. Unlike the other entries on this list, Masters of the Universe as a brand only dates back to 1982. Its parent company, Mattel , had created it to re-establish a foothold in the boys’ toy market, having already conquered the girls’ with Barbie. Given that the line was new, the Masters of the Universe action figures came with a mini-comic meant to introduce not only the individual toy’s character but also the larger lore around Eternia.

In the US, there was a plethora of Masters of the Universe comics, released from 1982 to 1987 across seven series rollouts. The comics predated the animated series, but the comic line would adjust starting in 1984 when there was a larger canon to contend with. DC Comics would take over production of the comics starting in 1983, with writer Gary Cohn taking over from Donald F. Glut.

From 1984 to 1985, the Super Powers collection from Kenner Toys published 23 mini-comics. These mini-comics included fan-favorite heroes such as Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman going up against the formidable Joker, Brainiac, and Lex Luthor. The second series focused on a broader base of heroes — Green Arrow, Dr. Fate, Firestorm, Martian Manhunter — than DC’s Trinity or Robin.

The Kenner toy line gave a big push for Jack Kirby’s “Fourth World”. Kirby’s “Fourth World” refers to Darkseid and his minions, characters that are instrumental in the DC Universe today. Kenner reached out to Kirby directly and had him commission designs for the action figures, such as Darkseid. A similar decision was made with George Perez when Kenner asked him to create a design for Cyborg.

While Super Powers started out as a toyline, it branched out into books, games, puzzles, toys, and was cross-branded with the Super Friends tv show. The mini-comics existed largely out of continuity, but Crisis on Infinite Earths: The Compendium classified the Super Powers world as Earth Thirty-Two. 

Which action figure mini-comics came as a surprise? Which were a no-brainer? Let us know in the comments below!

articles.title: You Can See Everything Is Hitting Box Office Milestones, But It’s Not Gonna Beat Out Michael Jackson (Hee Hee)
articles.summary: The documentary has been making tons of headlines.
articles.content:
The buzziest film on the 2026 movie schedule has to be You Can See Everything, and it just hit a major milestone by crossing the $100 million mark at the box office. For a movie that was made for a reported $7 million, it’s certainly one of the most successful A24 releases ever, but the Elizabeth Holmes documentary is nowhere close to the top-grossing documentary of all time, worldwide. That record belongs to the King of Pop himself for the posthumously released Michael Jackson : This Is It from 2009. How does it stack up to other documentaries? Well, it depends on how you count things.

You Can See Everything wasn’t quite the rocket ship that Fahrenheit 9/11 was out of the box, but it did a ton of steady business for weeks, finally topping the weekend box office in its third week of release . Now, after its release in the United Kingdom, the Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim-directed documentary has joined rarefied air as a documentary hitting that milestone. The $100 million mark slots You Can See Everyone into 7th worldwide.

That means the only two non-music and non-nature documentaries in the top ten are Fahrenheit 9/11 and You Can See Everything . It also means that You Can See Everything won’t be catching up to Michael Jackson. I don’t expect You Can See Everything to improve significantly at the worldwide box office. Elizabeth Holmes may be fascinating and infamous here, but Jackson was a massive star in every corner of the globe. In fact, domestically, This Is It actually trails You Can See Everything by almost $20 million.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Death is one of the few constants in life. Given how it's an unavoidable part of existence, it's no surprise that there's an endless number of works exploring all the different ways it can manifest. The newest upcoming project from Ignition Press is set to add to those numbers in a unique way , imagining a post-apocalyptic world where death has disastrous consequences. Dying has become the leading cause of death for everyone else left alive, and the drive to stay alive for the people who make life worth living is the main force pushing Pilgrimage Through Monsterland forward. This new comic follows a group of survivors as they trek their way across a ruined America, with survival being challenged in ways they couldn't have imagined.

Newbery Honor and Nebula Award-winning Lipan Apache writer Darcie Little Badger ( Elatsoe , Children of Owl ) is joined by incredible artist Kelsey Ramsay ( Dark Spaces: Good Deeds , Godzilla: Heist ) in crafting a story all about nature, death, and the love that pushes us to keep going. This story will have a major focus on the evolving dynamic between people and the world we live in, exploring the sprawling country through an Indigenous point of view, all while our protagonist tries to survive both the world and a serial killer. Pilgrimage Through Monsterland #1 hits store shelves on May 5, 2027, and ComicBook is honored to announce it all right here.

The main character, Nat, was an ordinary accountant living in LA when a curse befell humanity. Now, at the moment of death, corpses would transform into something entirely different. The lucky ones turned to stone, but others would mutate into horrible monsters, and some even unleashed devastating tornadoes, or something even worse. Wanting nothing more than to learn the fate of her sister, the last family she has left, Nat joined a group of survivors making their way to Texas. Between an entirely too enthusiastic guide, a group of familiar faces and strangers, monsters that stalk their steps, scavengers, and unnatural disasters, Nat learns that her problems are only just beginning, as she starts to think that one of her own is a murderer.

“ Pilgrimage Through Monsterland is the dark fantasy adventure I've always wanted to write,” said writer Darcie Little Badger. “What if death became a moment of transformation, unleashing tornadoes, monsters, and fire? How'd the world respond to this sudden, cataclysmic change in reality? The premise is Weird, but the core story is universal: at its heart, Pilgrimage Through Monsterland is about the lengths people go for family and survival. A group of strangers must rely on each other as they trek across a scarred and dangerous country, and Nat must trust that there's a home waiting for her on the other side…assuming she survives. Which, as the journey progresses, becomes increasingly unlikely. It's a professional dream to work with Kelsey, whose art captures the humanity of characters (and the horror of monsters and apocalyptic hellscapes). I'm so excited to see this project come to life.”

“ Pilgrimage Through Monsterland is such a meaningful project, giving a voice to stories untold, and it's a real honor to be involved,” said artist Kelsey Ramsay. “Darcie has managed to make every character feel so distinct, layered and complex, which has made bringing them to life on the page such a joy. I hope readers can recognize something of themselves in these characters and connect with the variety of people and personalities throughout the story. But, of course, I also hope they have an awesome time enjoying all the action, adventure and monster craziness along the way!”

This series is definitely a passionate project for Darcie Little Badger. Although she was born in Minnesota, she considers Texas her home, and her work in the Indigenous Futurisms movement always elevates her writing to the next level. This comic promises to bring a very unique perspective to the concept of death and our relationship with the world, drawing on Indigenous legends to tell a tale that's as invigorating as it is horrifying. This story will explore death in all its forms, and with the very idea of grief and despair being baked into the story's main threat, it's guaranteed to be a joy to read through.

Alongside Darcie Little Badger on the script and Kelsey Ramsay on the inks, the team is made up of colorist Tríona Farrell ( Showdown , Gotham City Sirens ) and letterer Ariana Maher ( Justice League Unlimited , Superman ). Additional details about Pilgrimage Through Monsterland will be released in early 2027, but be sure to guarantee you can snag your copy of the first issue at your local comic shop by pre-ordering before April 12, 2027.

Pilgrimage Through Monsterland releases on May 5, 2027!

articles.title: I Just Learned The Reason Vanna White Beat Out Hundreds Of Other Ladies For Wheel Of Fortune
articles.summary: She’s not the best letter-turner in the business for nothing!
articles.content:
It’s kind of hard to believe that Vanna White has been co-hosting Wheel of Fortune for nearly 45 years as of the 2026 television schedule . For thousands of episodes, White has been turning the iconic letter on the show, but her beginning was as humble as you would expect. In a recent appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon , White told the story of her audition, why she was chosen by legendary producer Merv Griffin, and even what her first puzzle was (and the first letter she turned).

I mean, yeah, fair enough, right? Though White’s role on the show has grown a lot over the years, far beyond only turning (now touching) the letters (and working hard for her salary ). In those early days, that was the job. If you’re going to get the gig, you better be elegant when you are flipping those lit-up boxes around! No one can argue with Griffin’s logic, and almost five incredible decades later, it's clear he couldn’t have made a better choice.

According to White, she’d wanted to be a TV star since she first saw her “uncle,” actor Christopher George, in an episode of his show The Rat Patrol in the mid ‘60s. George, it should be noted, was not a biological uncle, but was a close friend of her mother’s. On her first day filming, however, she was still quite nervous (and was even worried it wouldn't work out in the early days ), telling Fallon:

Famously, that wasn't the first time appearing on a game show. Two years before getting the job, she appeared as a contestant on The Price Is Right . Fallon and White talked about that appearance, which, sadly, ended without her making it on stage with Bob Barker, as she was never closest to the price of the item while on contestants' row.

Rising French R&B artist RnBoi, the first artist signed to Aya Nakamura’s label Nakamura Industrie, will be the inaugural musical guest and will perform a new track written for the show.

It includes Belgian-American actress, writer and director Bérangère McNeese, who spent part of her childhood in Kentucky and draws on both American and French comedy traditions; Daniel, best known for her Instagram character series “Les Caractères” and Canal+’s “Chamouxland”; Sawsan Abès, whose credits include “Ourika” and who is set to appear in the next season of “The White Lotus”; Emma Ebouaney, who’s built a following with her offbeat YouTube parodies, spoof reports and retro-inspired sketches; Bertrand Goncalves, who appeared in “Camembert” and Canal+’s “Super Plan,” hosted by Antoine de Caunes; François de Brauer, a theater performer known for his character-driven one-man shows, including “La Loi des prodiges”; and Luca Besse, whose credits include “Terrible Jungle.”

Eric Hannezo, head of programming, creative and development at Mediawan France and president of Black Dynamite and Mediawan Sport, pointed out that “comedy has long been part of our DNA.”

Hannezo previously produced “Le Débarquement,” an “SNL”-inspired sketch comedy show spearheaded by Jean Dujardin, Guillaume Canet and Gilles Lellouche, which aired two specials on Canal+ in 2013 and featured stars such as Marion Cotillard, as well as Alex Lutz and Payet himself.

articles.title: OG Christmas Vacation Director Gets Real About How Feud With Chevy Chase Made Him Quit The Film
articles.summary: Chris Columbus needed the job, but not badly enough to work with Chevy Chase.
articles.content:
Chris Columbus directed Home Alone , but he came remarkably close to spending Christmas with the Griswolds instead. Before that movie became a holiday staple, he was supposed to direct National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation . Then he met Chevy Chase, and Columbus' latest account makes his decision to walk away sound even gutsier than I realized.

Columbus was coming off 1988's Heartbreak Hotel , which left him convinced his directing career might be over. He'd returned to Chicago and was staying with his in-laws when John Hughes called . The Christmas Vacation offer was supposed to get him back behind the camera, and he'd already started shooting second-unit footage.

The filmmaker has spoken harshly about Chase before . But this time, he said he's less interested in adding to the actor's bad press . Then he recalled how things reached the point where he called Hughes and quit:

I appreciate that Columbus is making room for a little perspective here. He didn't suddenly declare the feud resolved or pretend the experience was pleasant. He just sounds tired of spending another interview beating up Chase. Fair enough. I'd be tired of telling that story, too, especially knowing it started with a job he desperately needed. But the Harry Potter franchise filmmaker continued:

Jeremiah S. Chechik took over Christmas Vacation , and Home Alone arrived in theaters in 1990. I'm grateful both movies became Christmas classics , although it's amusing to imagine what Columbus might have done with Clark Griswold's disastrous holiday lighting display. Given those early meetings, I suspect he'd rather not imagine it at all.

articles.title: Star Trek Once Reused a Monster From Another Classic Sci-Fi Series & Almost Nobody Noticed
articles.summary: The aliens of Star Trek had to look convincing to viewers on a reasonably low budget before the franchise became one of the most popular and successful sci-fi franchises on TV. This meant a fair bit of ingenuity when it came to costumes, makeup, and utilizing whatever the studio could use. Which, as it turns […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The aliens of Star Trek had to look convincing to viewers on a reasonably low budget before the franchise became one of the most popular and successful sci-fi franchises on TV. This meant a fair bit of ingenuity when it came to costumes, makeup, and utilizing whatever the studio could use. Which, as it turns out, included more than a little inspiration from another sci-fi show.

A strange yet fascinating example occurred when an alien life form from another TV show helped inspire a creature encountered by the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise. The most surprising thing about this reference is that it wasn't simply a case of one alien looking similar to another. In fact, one talented creature performer used his craftsmanship to create practical aliens while helping keep production costs down. It's one of those revelations that becomes even more interesting when you consider how much old sci-fi TV regularly borrowed from one another.

The link can be traced back to The Outer Limits , which played host to scores of strange life-forms during its 1963 to 1965 run. One of these was encountered in the 1965 episode "The Probe." This creature was a giant alien microbe brought to life by stuntman, actor, and creature designer Janos Prohaska. And this is where it gets a bit more complicated. Prohaska would later bring his creature-making skills to Star Trek , designing and wearing the costume of one of the franchise's strangest aliens. Who would have thought a monster from another great sci-fi TV series would help inspire one of Star Trek 's most iconic encounters?

That fiend was the Horta in "The Devil in the Dark." Prohaska constructed and performed in the suit himself, and demonstrated the creature's movements for producer Gene L. Coon, helping inspire the episode's story. No, the connection isn't simply that the original Outer Limits costume was dragged over to the Enterprise without any changes. Rather, Prohaska modified his earlier giant microbe costume, adding details such as veins and a fringe to create the Horta's distinctive appearance. Pretty clever bit of sci-fi TV trivia, if you think about it. The very same guy who helped bring one weird alien to life on The Outer Limits went on to bring us another one on Star Trek . And if you've ever wondered how Star Trek came up with so many wonderfully bizarre monsters in the '60s, there you go: it all came down, in part, to one talented creature performer and one very unusual costume.

Of course, Star Trek was not the only sci-fi show in town. TV budgets in the 1960s were not unlimited, and not every episode warranted a new alien costume or piece of makeup. Borrowing an existing costume or appliance was a reasonable fix. This was especially true considering that some of the same creative people worked on both shows. Makeup artist Fred Phillips worked on both productions, supervising makeup for The Outer Limits before taking on the same role for Star Trek . His involvement in both series is another example of how closely connected these classic television productions could be.

And the Anthropoid Ape wasn't the only Star Trek creature with a connection to The Outer Limits . The humanoid bird seen in "The Cage" has a particularly interesting connection to the Megasoid from "The Duplicate Man." The costume is believed to have been reused for the Star Trek creature, although some details were changed. The Anthropoid Ape from the same pilot also had a connection to The Outer Limits : its facial piece had previously appeared on the Calco creature in the episode "Fun and Games," paired with a different furry costume. It's another fun example of how these classic sci-fi productions shared more than just a love of strange-looking aliens. Sometimes, a monster could find a second life on an entirely different television show. Not a bad career move for a creature from the 1960s.

This took quite a bit of digging, and there are plenty of sources and behind-the-scenes details on the subject. If I missed something or you have another interesting detail to add, let me know! Now, join the away team in the comments: Did you know about this Star Trek connection, and what other recycled creatures or props have you spotted across the franchise? Let's hear it!

An ITN spokeswoman said: "ITN does not use NDAs to prevent people talking openly about their experiences with the company, including at Channel 4 News. We stopped using confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements in 2022, and also lifted them from the small number of people who had previously been subject to them. We have listened and learned, and apologised where we have got things wrong in the past."

Discussion about NDAs has returned to the fore in UK entertainment after Russell Brand was sentence to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault and allegations about David Walliams were published by The Guardian and ITN-operated ITV News, allegations that Walliams vehemently denies. Both celebrities were reported to have used NDAs, prompting British ministers to look into ways they can quickly change the law to expand protections that stop NDAs being used to cover up harassment or discrimination. These protections are being implemented via the new Employment Rights Act.

The UK's influential Digital, Culture, Media & Sport Committee has annonced a high-profile probe into industry NDA use, with evidence sessions set to begin in two weeks. Witnesses and timings will be announced shortly and it feels highly likely that executives from ITN or Channel 4 will be invited to speak. Separately, Channel 4, where Brand used to host shows, has been under pressure for historic NDA use, with CEO Priya Dogra telling the committee last week that the network uses confidentality clauses in a limited way with “pretty large caveats." articles.title: The Punisher Just Made the Ultimate Argument Against Spider-Man's No-Kill Rule

While that is the go-to argument for killing villains, Spider-Man has the same code in Marvel Comics. That same argument was brought up in a new comic where the Punisher told Spider-Man why his […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Everyone loves to talk about Batman's no-kill rule and how it always results in villains coming back to kill more people. While that is the go-to argument for killing villains, Spider-Man has the same code in Marvel Comics. That same argument was brought up in a new comic where the Punisher told Spider-Man why his refusal to kill villains will always come back to haunt him. The series is Punisher vs. The Amazing Spider-Man , and it had Spider-Man and the Punisher reluctantly teaming up, with each hero believing he could convince the other that his way was better. That all came to a head in the final issue of the miniseries.

In Punisher vs. The Amazing Spider-Man #5 (2026) by Dan Abnett and Alvaro Lopez, the Punisher learned that the woman he was working with, Smokeshow, was a villain and was using him all along. With the Punisher gunning to bring her down, Spider-Man rushed into action to stop him. In the end, the Punisher called out Spider-Man for claiming to want to save everyone while allowing all his villains to live, which puts everyone in danger.

Smokeshow was shocked when she saw that the Punisher was gunning for her, and she didn't understand why at first, until she realized Frank Castle had discovered the truth. This was the ultimate betrayal for Frank since he served with Smokeshow in the Marines, and he thought she was helping him get rid of drug cartels, but she was really clearing out the competition and was leading her own cartel as well. The Punisher was rushing in, with the intent of killing everyone. That is when Spider-Man showed up to stop him.

This led to Spider-Man fighting the Punisher , even as he gunned his way through the office building, trying to reach Smokeshow. It started when Spider-Man webbed the gun out of Frank's hand before he could execute a man. Spider-Man said no one dies, and the Punisher opened fire on Spider-Man before racing up the stairs. This eventually led to Spider-Man reaching Smokeshow first, and he saved her by webbing the Punisher before he could kill her, although he was too late to stop Frank from killing Smokeshow's main enforcer. When Frank killed the man, Spider-Man knocked Frank out for the count.

This is what then led to their big conversation about what makes the two men different. Spider-Man said he made a big mistake by believing that he could trust the Punisher. He then said things weren't funny anymore, and he told Smokeshow to turn herself in. Then he told the Punisher he was going to jail too and apologized for not being able to help him. That made Frank say Spider-Man couldn't because he was just being Spider-Man and Frank was being the Punisher. They were never a good fit. He then said Spider-Man would lose every time he got in a fight with a villain.

This led to the argument that when a hero like Batman or Spider-Man allows the villains to live and sends them to jail every time, they would always come back to hurt them. When Spider-Man said he would never kill, the Punisher said that meant he lost every time. He said Spider-Man will beat the villains, and they will get up again. He said if Spider-Man were serious, he would see that he was never stopping the villains from hurting anyone else. To make his point, Frank said Spider-Man should kill him.

This shocked Spider-Man, but the Punisher pressed on. He said jail won't stop him, and if Spider-Man doesn't kill him, the Punisher will always be back, "just like every freak in your costume-parade life." Spider-Man asked if it was a threat, and the Punisher said it was just a "statement of fact." The Punisher said that Spider-Man would risk his life to stop the villains and then let them live, and they would always come back for more. The Punisher said that he would come back for more.

Spider-Man then said that Frank was smart and rational, and he doesn't understand why Frank doesn't get it. The Punisher responded bluntly that he is smart and rational and that "friendly" will only get Spider-Man so far. While the Punisher is right, Spider-Man is also a man of strong morals, so this was never going to work. That said, it was also a case of Spider-Man likely knowing that the Punisher was going to escape, since he had given Frank some web solvent earlier, Frank escaped, saying that Spider-Man would never finish what he started. On the other hand, the Punisher said he would finish what Spider-Man can't.

What are your thoughts on the Punisher vs. The Amazon Spider-Man series ? Let us know your thoughts on the Punisher's description of Spider-Man in the comments below.

articles.title: 5 Movie Businesses That Would Be Absolutely Miserable Places to Work
articles.summary: We've all been there. Your boss is a power-hungry mutant tyrant, your coworkers are robots, and you're stuck in a job that makes you reconsider every decision you've ever made in your entire life. Ok, maybe that's a bit exaggerated. But even our jobs aren't so bad that we have to worry about getting eaten […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google We've all been there. Your boss is a power-hungry mutant tyrant, your coworkers are robots, and you're stuck in a job that makes you reconsider every decision you've ever made in your entire life. Ok, maybe that's a bit exaggerated. But even our jobs aren't so bad that we have to worry about getting eaten by dinosaurs, catching a deadly disease, or being blown up by our shady boss. When you think of some of Hollywood's best-known fictional companies and organizations, it's a miracle anyone would ever want to work for them.

Some of these companies might appear mighty impressive on the surface. They've got buckets of cash, tech know-how, slick headquarters, and seemingly unlimited resources. But look beneath the surface, and you'll find some truly terrible places to work. From a possible Fortune 500 company to an military force bent on conquering the galaxy, here are five fictional organizations you would not want to get a job with. And honestly, some of these bosses are worse than your standard nightmare boss.

Serving in the Ministry of Magic is pretty much a dream job if you happen to be a Harry Potter fan. How amazing would it be to work every day among witches and wizards, magical beasties, and spells? You'd be able to use some of the most awesome tech around. Well, it's magic, and we bet you'd see some stuff that would make the average person on the street go weak at the knees. But there's a dark side to this stunning workplace.

First of all, the organization itself has a rather dubious past of corruption, stupidity, and political meddling. As an employee, you'll be faced with mountains of administrative rubbish, unstable leadership, and the sudden threat of having the Ministry taken over by a dark wizard's followers. Just look at what happens when Voldemort's followers seize control of the Ministry: suddenly, it's business as usual for those of us in the civil service, but now we have to work in fear of a regime that goes around hurting innocent people. And Dolores Umbridge as your boss? You might as well just resign. I think I would prefer to work in a Muggle office with a broken coffee machine.

Who wouldn't want to work in Jurassic Park? Just think about it: playing with living dinosaurs all day long. You'd also be studying them and making history. You could have one of the most awesome jobs out there and get to see dinosaurs that had been extinct for millions of years. Yet there's a big catch: the dinosaurs are unpredictable, and some of them would not think twice about having you for a meal.

Jurassic Park makes it very clear that John Hammond's dream isn't exactly the safest place to work. His employees face angry dinosaurs, faulty security systems, and management decisions that seem to go out of their way to ignore clear safety hazards. And after Dennis Nedry sabotages the park's computer systems, its security infrastructure begins to collapse, leaving employees and visitors vulnerable to dinosaurs roaming beyond their enclosures. Personally, I'd never want to be the unfortunate security guard called to the scene of a velociraptor on the loose. And as much as I think dinosaurs are the coolest things ever, I think I'd prefer being a tourist rather than risking my entire dinosaur-loving career on Jurassic Park.

OCP (also known as Omni Consumer Products) is one of those imaginary companies that sounds great until you dig a little deeper. OCP has enormous influence over Detroit in RoboCop and is doing all kinds of work, from the production of consumer goods to funding the police department. The company has huge visions for the city's future, but its business ethics are questionable.

Firstly, I would not want to work for OCP as I believe it employs its workers as disposable commodities, and that the company and its executives are focused far more on money than they are on people's lives. When police officer Alex Murphy is brutally murdered by Clarence Boddicker's gang, OCP doesn't simply let him rest in peace. Instead, executive Bob Morton selects Murphy for the RoboCop project, using his body to create a corporate experiment that turns a murdered police officer into a machine. I would also not work for a company where the boss thinks it is acceptable to use your body as a test subject if it suited the company's interests. Not to mention that Dick Jones has the sort of corporate management style that would make me think long and hard before agreeing to work for OCP.

There are a lot of advantages to being an employee of the Galactic Empire : you're exposed to the cutting-edge technology of the galaxy, have access to large military facilities, and get to work in the service of the most powerful galactic government. However, there are a few downsides, of course. Darth Vader is your boss, and your employer is a tyrannical government. And one mistake could be the end of your career—or your life.

Just try to put yourself in the shoes of an average Imperial officer and see how that day goes. You're probably in one of the most perilous jobs in the galaxy. It's hard not to get the vibe that anyone, even in the Imperial workforce, would be terrified of making the smallest mistake. And you'd be sharing that workplace with stormtroopers, military leaders, and who knows who else. Any of them would probably be pretty upset if they found out Darth Vader had wandered into your department. And then there's the small matter of the Death Star. Twice, the Empire managed to build a gigantic, enormously expensive space station, only to have it destroyed by the Rebel Alliance. Imagine being one of the thousands of Imperial personnel stationed aboard when that happened. That's one redundancy package you definitely wouldn't want! Those uniforms are nice and all, but I don't think free healthcare would be enough to get me to join!

The one I'd least like to work for, and I really can't come up with many other fictional employers that would be more ghastly than the Umbrella Corporation. The public side is a huge multinational pharmaceutical corporation with state-of-the-art research facilities and deep pockets; the private side is all about horrifying experiments, including bioweapons, lethal viruses, and scientific projects that could turn your average day at the office into a complete nightmare.

Imagine arriving at work one morning to discover that a biological experiment has gone horribly wrong and your colleagues are turning into flesh-eating zombies. That's essentially what happens in the Resident Evil universe , where Umbrella's secret research into the T-virus leads to catastrophic outbreaks. And guess what? The company has an even more dubious record of covering up its misdeeds than it does of trying to save the day. One day, you might be in a perfectly normal office, and the next, you're fighting for your life. I'd also wonder whether I'd really want a job where the security staff seems more concerned with guarding company secrets than with saving the lives of employees. The pay would have to be out of this world, right? No, actually, no job is worth being a zombie.

AFFI made its debut in Mumbai in 2011, backed by Hugh […]
articles.content:
The Australian Film Festival of India (AFFI) is back after a COVID-era hiatus, staging screenings across Indian cities through Dec. 22 alongside a new industry strand aimed at pulling Indian producers and investors toward Australia as the India-Australia Audio Visual Co-Production Treaty takes effect.

AFFI made its debut in Mumbai in 2011, backed by Hugh Jackman, and later editions drew support from Baz Luhrmann and Phillip Noyce. Festival director Peter Castaldi now oversees the relaunch. Sitting on its advisory council are producer Lori Fesker, actor-producer Viveck Vaswani, and Vinod Daniel OAM and Sonia Gandhi, both cultural leaders from the Indian Australian community. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade at 100: Massive Minions, K-Pop Stars and ‘Sorcerer’s Apprentice’ Mickey Mouse

The centerpiece of the industry push is the Screen Australia-backed Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which will run full-day sessions in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum, with more cities to be added. The sessions are pitched at Indian producers and directors as well as investors, distributors, students and VFX and post houses. Topics include co-producing under the new treaty, putting money into Australian films and India-focused Australian projects, government and state incentives such as the Producer Offset, cross-border distribution, and access to Australian VFX, post-production, locations and specialist crews.

Money is a big part of the pitch. Australia's Producer Offset refunds 40% of qualifying local spend on eligible feature films, and states offer their own grants and attraction funds. Together, the incentives lower how much capital investors put at risk.

"This is an exciting time to strengthen screen industry ties between Australia and India," said Grainne Brunsdon, Screen Australia's chief operating officer. "Having had a delegation of producers at WAVES Film Bazaar , Screen Australia is proud to support this series of Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which provides filmmakers from Australia and India with more opportunities to connect, collaborate and create new pathways for stories that celebrate the richness and diversity of our shared cultural connections." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Disney Studios, Ausfilm, the City of Perth and the University of NSW are among the institutions supporting the festival itself. Ausfilm CEO Kate Marks said the organization welcomed moves to draw the two industries closer and, as Australia's film commission, was on hand to help Indian filmmakers make use of the country's production and post-production capabilities. "Initiatives like Screen Australia's delegation to Goa and the Australian Film Festival of India are a great way to build connections and open the door to more collaboration," she said.

On the screening side, the lineup features "First Light," Australia's official submission for the international feature Oscar; "Brand Bollywood Downunder," from AFFI founding creative director Anupam Sharma, which features well-known names from the Indian film business; and "UnIndian," starring Brett Lee. Indian-origin Australians including producer Chetan Oberoi and Yogi Devgan will also be showcased.

"Indian cinema has conquered the world on its own terms. Australia offers Indian storytellers something rare: a bigger canvas, world-class crews and post-production, government support which reduces financial risks in the film, and a system that delivers on time and on budget," said Sharma. "We want to see Indian money, Indian stories and Australian know-how in the same film, on screens around the world."

Partners in several Indian cities have signed on. The International Film Festival of Kerala will present a handpicked slate of Australian titles and a panel, while Shanmugam and AVM Studios will host the Chennai leg.

"The showcase brings the best of new Australian cinema to Indian audiences," said Castaldi, who added that AFFI is also putting a spotlight on the expanding pool of Australian screen talent with Indian roots.

Sharda hasn't been officially cast as Sthalekar, though she says the cricketer would like her to play the role. "And the other producers on board, who I can't reveal right now, probably would," she adds.

Sharda launched Bodhini in 2024, naming it after the feminine of the Bodhi tree. "As a French-speaking actress, I never thought that I would get the chance to use that skill," Sharda says. "It's a dream for any actor to be able to lead a film where you have to have that one-on-one lock-in time with your director, and it really is the medium of storytelling and filmmaking in its purest form."

On a possible return to mainstream Bollywood, Sharda says: "I have really started to miss it because I'm so Indian. Speaking in Hindi, speaking in kind of the lilts of my Indian self is something I miss."

articles.title: Chris Evans’ Return in Avengers: Doomsday Has Already Spoiled Steve Rogers’ Perfect Arc
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Avengers: Endgame felt like an event for many reasons. It was the culmination of the Infinity Saga, finally pitting Earth’s Mightiest Heroes against Thanos for one last showdown. Aside from its main villain, the plot of the film was shrouded in mystery, with fans left unaware that it all hinged on a journey through the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Endgame felt like an event for many reasons. It was the culmination of the Infinity Saga , finally pitting Earth’s Mightiest Heroes against Thanos for one last showdown. Aside from its main villain, the plot of the film was shrouded in mystery, with fans left unaware that it all hinged on a journey through the MCU via a “time heist” to retrieve the Infinity Stones and undo the devastating ending of Avengers: Infinity War . It also seemed to be the final Marvel film for both Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans , who had anchored the MCU for roughly a decade as the co-leaders of the Avengers franchise. Now both Downey and Evans are back for Avengers: Doomsday , which inevitably raises a ton of questions.

Of course, Downey’s and Evans’ returns couldn’t be more different. After his Tony Stark sacrificed himself to save the universe, Downey is back in the MCU fold this time as Victor von Doom, the titular villain of Avengers: Doomsday . This has left fans puzzling over how, if at all, the MCU’s Doctor Doom will connect to Tony Stark, a question made more confusing by what Marvel has said about the character. Meanwhile, Evans is seemingly back as the same Steve Rogers fans know and love — with magic, time travel, and the multiverse in the mix, who can be sure? — but no matter what Avengers: Doomsday does, the character’s arc has already been spoiled.

In one of their first interactions, Tony Stark and Steve Rogers call each other out. Stark claims that Rogers is only special because of the Super Soldier Serum, while Rogers accuses him of never being willing to lay his own life on the line to save others. But throughout their time on the Avengers together, the two heroes prove each other wrong . Tony is actually the one who makes the sacrifice play, using the Infinity Stones to defeat Thanos and his army at the expense of his own life. And not only is Steve worthy of lifting Mjolnir, but he takes the opportunity to lay down his shield and pursue a life with his beloved Peggy Carter. Here is the original ending of Avengers: Endgame :

Despite the early MCU very much figuring out what it wants to be in real time, the Infinity Saga managed to give its two lead heroes the perfect farewell. After seven films — not including his several uncredited cameos — as Steve Rogers, Evans walked away from Marvel with a sense of completion and satisfaction. By the end of 2019’s Avengers: Endgame , Steve finally gets that dance he promised Peggy in 2011’s Captain America: The First Avenger . And in that moment, the Infinity Saga ends not with an epic battle sequence and not a gotcha stinger teasing what comes next. Instead, it ends on an intimate moment between two characters who have overcome impossible odds for the chance to be together.

Then Avengers Endgame: Encore happened. Among the only new additions to the rerelease is an altered ending that interrupts Steve and Peggy’s hard-earned dance with a knock at the door. It’s Loki, seemingly there to warn them of Doctor Doom’s imminent plans. Cue the events of Avengers: Doomsday . While it might be there to retcon a direct connection between the fourth and fifth Avengers films, this change undercuts everything that has happened in the MCU since, including the pitch-perfect conclusion of Steve’s arc. In a flash, that cathartic ending of Avengers: Endgame is compromised to satisfy the storytelling needs of the larger shared universe. Still, it remains to be seen where Avengers: Doomsday goes from here.

Fans only get a tease of what Steve Rogers — likely officially adopting the Nomad moniker this time — is up to in the fight against Doctor Doom. So it’s anyone’s guess how this all plays out. Likely, if Doom is tied to Stark somehow, Steve is there to emotionally react to his departed friend’s face on this new threat. But it’s very possible that things aren’t exactly as they seem. Marvel has a long history of purposefully misleading fans to preserve the theatrical experience. Will Steve immediately walk away from Peggy to join the fight? Is this even the Steve we know? Or are there some multiversal shenanigans afoot? But for now, the MCU has tarnished Steve and Peggy’s happy ending. Here’s hoping he gets right back to dancing as soon as this latest adventure is over.

Did Marvel ruin the ending of Avengers: Endgame ? If so, can the MCU still recover Steve and Peggy’s happy ending? Let us know in the comments below!

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18, 2026.

They added they would be a "hands-on and results-driven advisory team of seasoned specialists, helping C-suites, boards, founders and investors work out what is stopping them scaling and delivering real, smart and swift solutions."

Abbott will provide IP, studios and transformational and operational infrastructure advice. She was most recently the Chief Content Officer at The Earthshot Prize, Prince William's environmental initiative. He is now a non-exec director of The Podcast Show and subscription platform SupaPas.

Glynne is the branded entertainment and IP strategy expert. She founded and was head of UTA's EMEA Entertainment and Culture Marketing business, and worked as Global SVP of Branded Entertainment at Fremantle, working across 30 territories. Prior to that, she ran Renault TV and set up and ran The Audio Channel for All3Media and BBH. She's also a Cannes Lions judge.

Smales, considered by many the architect of the creator economy and influencer world in Europe, will focus on talent and the creator economy solutions. He's known for leading Gleam Futures, the early digital-first talent management business he founded in 2010. In 2021, he exited for Dentsu and now runs WinnieWood, a creator economy group that spans talent management, entertainment IP, commerce, tech and investments, and is a co-founder of creator-led entertainment producer GloMotion Studios.

Turajlic will handle digital transformation and entrepreneurship. She is known as co-founder of Little Dot Studios alongside the late Andy Taylor. articles.title: India-Chile Co-Production Treaty Nears Final Stage as Chilean Producers Court Indian Partners at IFFI Goa (EXCLUSIVE)

articles.content:
An audiovisual co-production treaty between India and Chile has reached the last stage of negotiation, according to Jorge Loyola Castro, Chile's trade commissioner to India, who spoke to Variety at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The talks trace back to then-President Gabriel Boric's state visit to India in April 2025, the first by a Chilean president since Michelle Bachelet's trip in 2009. Castro says the visit set the co-production negotiations in motion. In a joint statement issued during the trip, Boric and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi named audiovisual co-production among the areas where the two countries would look to work together. José Antonio Kast succeeded Boric as president in March. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Narnia' White Witches Tilda Swinton and Emma Mackey Excited to Meet for the First Time at Marrakech Film Festival: 'My Absolute Dream' Claes Bang, Emma Mackey, Vicky Krieps and More Join Marion Cotillard in Marrakech Jury

"It has been started and now is at the final, final stage, so we hope that we can bring some news soon," Loyola tells Variety .

There is no firm date yet. Loyola points out that the process only began last year, adding: "We really, really hope that by next year we can announce something. If something happens earlier, more than happy, but it's a priority for Chile as well."

The treaty is moving alongside a broader trade pact, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The two sides finalized its terms of reference during Boric's visit and have held four rounds of talks since, the most recent in New Delhi in December 2025, according to India's embassy in Santiago. India's commerce secretary traveled to Chile in August to advance the negotiations. Bilateral trade grew from $3.84 billion in 2024 to $5.38 billion in 2025, with Indian imports of Chilean gold accounting for much of the rise. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Chilean producers are already lining up. Giancarlo Nasi, producer and CEO of Quijote Films, which operates out of Santiago and Los Angeles, came off a strong 2025. Quijote produced Diego Céspedes' "The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo," winner of the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes, and co-produced Gabriel Mascaro's Brazilian drama "The Blue Trail," which took the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin.

"I love pushing the boundaries of what is possible and doing the craziest co-production that you can find. So co-producing with India would be ideal," Nasi says.

Without a treaty, Quijote gets around the gap by bringing in a partner from a third country that has a treaty with Chile. A French company on Ukrainian drama "Pamfir," which played Cannes in 2022, allowed Quijote to tap the Chilean-French treaty. A French company was also attached early on to John Trengove's South African drama "The Smell of Apples," which premiered at Toronto in September, and a French producer is on board the documentary Quijote is now making with Moroccan filmmaker Asmae El Moudir, who shared Cannes' documentary prize for "The Mother of All Lies" in 2023.

A direct treaty would remove that detour. Nasi says the key is for Chile to build "a minoritarian co-production fund that is bigger and bigger and stronger so it can actually make a difference for an Indian production."

A fan of Indian cinema since childhood, Nasi cites "RRR" and "The Lunchbox" as proof of its range. He has been receiving Indian projects, but has yet to find the right one. Many come from Indian filmmakers living in the U.S. who want to tell stories of migration and return, often on mid-sized budgets with no state funding available to them. He would like to make a film that spans India, the U.S. and Chile.

"There's a crisis in the States in terms of financing independent movies because the distribution system of independent movies is changing," Nasi says. "Theaters are more and more reserved to horror genre movies or big movies, so the independent dramas, they're having trouble finding a place."

Chile's factual sector is also in the hunt. Miguel Soffia, founder and director of Santiago-based We Are South, who has spent 15 years producing factual content with streamers and broadcasters around the world, is drawing up deal memos and contracts with a company he met at the market that is behind a hornbill film. The project is a natural history co-production about big cats – the puma, the snow leopard and the Eurasian lynx – spanning India, the Andes and Europe. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"We ran into a company here that was brilliant. They were doing the same stuff as us and it was just serendipity," Soffia says.

The project follows "Extremes of the Americas," a six-part series on climate change that We Are South co-produced with Canada and shot in northern Canada and southern Chile. Soffia is also developing a Pacific Ring of Fire project connecting Japan, the Philippines, Tahiti and New Zealand with the Americas through earthquakes, tsunamis and volcanoes, and has a potential Canadian co-producer at the market.

Talking to Malaysian contacts, Soffia found that they share myths with Indigenous communities back home, in which oxen cause earthquakes in a struggle between land and sea. "Of course, there's a science basis to it, but there's also a massive cultural phenomenon and human experience in common that we want to explore in that film," he says.

As for Quijote's next step once a treaty is signed: "Do a lot of Indian movies," Nasi says.

The feature is a family drama centering on a troubled mother-son relationship and a simple family gathering that fast derails.

Variety’s reviewer Jessica Kiang wrote, “A droll dramedy of bourgeois social awkwardness morphs into a deep-cut tragedy about the effects of a mother’s psychological frailty on her grown-up children, in Danish director Mads Mengel‘s impressively uncozy debut.”

articles.title: 5 Spider-Man: The Animated Series Storylines That Deserve to Be in the MCU
articles.summary: With Spider-Man: Brand New Day as Tom Holland's fourth solo film, the Marvel Cinematic Universe has now featured more Spider-Man stories on the big screen than any previous iteration. That's the case without even mentioning his appearances in larger MCU projects alongside other heroes. The thing about Spider-Man is that he has so many great […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google With Spider-Man: Brand New Day as Tom Holland's fourth solo film, the Marvel Cinematic Universe has now featured more Spider-Man stories on the big screen than any previous iteration. That's the case without even mentioning his appearances in larger MCU projects alongside other heroes. The thing about Spider-Man is that he has so many great tales and storylines that they could keep making highly entertaining movies about him for as long as they want. A good place to look for inspiration is Spider-Man: The Animated Series from the '90s . The show has withstood the test of time as a legitimate classic superhero series.

Seeing some of the spectacular stories from the show come to life in the MCU would be incredible. However, there are some great ones that wouldn't entirely fit into the franchise. "Six Forgotten Warriors" features an odd mix of characters for the MCU, while the Man-Spider arc known as "Neogenic Nightmare" was kind of touched upon in Spider-Man: Brand New Day . There's also the Secret Wars arc that is clealry going to be part of Avengers: Secret Wars , so that's out of the question. Thankfully, Spider-Man: The Animated Series has plenty of other great stories the MCU could pull from.

Spider-Wars is the kind of story that feels ripe for adaptation in the Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse franchise but the MCU could do something fun with it too. This was the closing arc of the '90s series and it sees the main Spider-Man parnter up with several variations from the multiverse. That is basically the premise for Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse , but this one also involved characters like Madame Web and The Beyonder.

It would be interesting to see Tom Holland's Spider-Man join forces again with Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield while also throwing in a couple of other brand new variants. The MCU would also be able to introduce its own version of Madame Web after the Sony movie flopped. These Spider-Men come together to take on a Spider-Carnage variant and that's a villain who would be incredible to see on the big screen. Watching a Peter deal with a symbiote that isn't Venom sounds refreshing.

The combination of Spider-Man and Dardevil is one that just makes too much sense. Both are street-level heroes based out of New York and their personalities make for great entertainment. Spidey is more lighthearted and quippy, while Daredevil is more serious and stoic, which is a tremendous combination. The "Man Without Fear" episodes of Spider-Man: The Animated Series played into that dynamic while also involving characters like Kingpin.

Kingpin is a major antagonist for both heroes and Vincent D'Onofrio's performance as the character in the MCU makes him someone we always want more of. This story sees Kingpin's son frame Peter Parker for treason and the MCU could do the same but with just Kingpin behind it. Matt Murdock becomes Peter's lawyer, putting them on the same team both in and out of their superhero alter egos. The show also delivered a fun twist as it was J. Jonah Jameson who paid Murdock to defend Peter, which shows a different side of Jameson, though that's unlikely in an MCU adaptation.

Despite the many iterations of Spider-Man in movies over the years, Black Cat is a character who hasn't appeared to date. The closest we came was Felicity Jones as Felicia Hardy in a small part in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 , which never grew into more. Seeing someone bring Hardy to life in the MCU would be fantastic and would feel fresh, especially if the franchise is moving past the Peter and MJ relationship.

Even if they aren't, there's a lot of drama that can be pulled from Peter trying to reconnect with MJ while spending time with the increasingly flirtatious Black Cat . The "Partners in Danger" arc showcases Hardy's origin story and sees her work with Peter, despite also being an antagonist. Watching Peter grapple with being pulled towards MJ and Felicia is an intriguing dynamic to see play out, as is seeing Peter deal with the fact that Felicia is a criminal at heart.

One of the wildest things that Spider-Man: The Animated Series pulled off was reveal that Mary Jane was a clone. The character was written off for a while and returned to Peter's shock and happiness. The two got married and went on their honeymoon, which was interrupted by MJ's ex-boyfriend, Morrie Bench. Morrie had become Hydro-Man , which is a villain who would be cool to see in live-action, especially given how a similar character looked in Spider-Man: Far From Home .

The story ultimately led to Peter finding out that the Mary Jane he married is actually a clone, while the real MJ who he initially fell in love with is lost in the multiverse. The MCU adapting this would play into the multiverse stories they're telling and would mark another bit of heartbreak for Peter, which is a staple of his character. The show famously saw the cloned MJ evaporate, meaning Peter loses her once again. The love that fans have for Holland and Zendaya's takes on the characters would make this extra emotional.

Venom has been brought to the screen a lot over the years but we haven't had enough Carnage. Putting them together in the MCU for an arc from the animated series would be ideal, especially given how this story plays out. As part of the "Sins of the Father" episodes, the danger that Carnage poses to everyone forces Spider-Man and Venom to team up, which is an easy sell for the MCU since Venom is already so popular. Seeing their relationship in a different light would be a welcome sight.

This "Sins of the Father" storyline also fits for the MCU because it brought so many characters together, which we know is something the franchise loves to do. Elements of the arc involve Doctor Strange, Mordo, Dormammu, Iron Man, and War Machine. While the MCU can't make all of that happen, it would give a chance for Spider-Man to team up with Doctor Strange again, play into the abandoned Mordo storyline, and give us fresh takes on Venom and Carnage.

Are there any other storylines from Spider-Man: The Animated Series that you'd like to see in the MCU? Let us know in the comments!

articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE: For Fin Taylor , one half of the satirical podcast Fin Vs History , there's no going back to TV now.

The British stand-up comedian, writer and podcaster, who fronts his show with fellow comedian Horatio Gould , had over the years made appearances on staple British comedy shows such as Live at the Apollo and The Last Leg , but his deliberately shocking style didn't feel like a good fit – to him.

As we sit down for lunch at the Ham Yard Hotel in London, he recalls making a VT for BBC news satire The Mash Report that had been cut so severely that it made his deliberately anti-woke character seemed more "fascist" than a satirical take on a news reporter. He was livid. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Executives Reed Hastings On Netflix Shakeup, YouTube Rivalry And How Streamer Can Go Back To "Being Thrilling" News Sue Perkins Exploring ADHD Diagnosis For First Time In Audible Podcast 'Attention, Please! "This was during Covid, when agents weren’t allowed to come to the record," he recalls. "I went into the gallery and I threw my toys out of the pram, and said, ‘You can’t use that in the show.’ I had basically accepted I wouldn’t be asked back, but weirdly they called the next morning and apologized, and they got me to write more stuff for them."
